acceptance: Whether an Agent is at work is read from its sessions: an open session counts, and so does the pause of up to two minutes between a running task's connections; a lapsed lease nobody closed does not, even with a command recorded as running; another Agent's sessions are never credited. On a server that reports commands, being connected is not being at work: only a running command (or the pause between two) counts, and the last command — not when the connection opened or closed — is when it last worked. Sessions that could not be read are distinguished from there being none. The status reads Working now, Last worked <time>, or No recent work, and nothing when unknown.

The Header's Agents follow the server: an Agent shows once it is allowed and goes once it is removed, and so do the Agents asking to join (none from a server that predates requests); a refresh reads at once rather than at the next poll. The list is read every ten seconds, every three while someone waits on an Agent (an open dialog or an invite out) and back to ten after; a hidden window is not polled and catches up when it returns. A bad network keeps what is known; a 403 forgets the Agents and requests and stops asking for good, including on the very first read. An Agent whose activity could not be read is still listed. Without a target nothing is asked and whatever the last target held is forgotten, and an answer overtaken by a newer read never shows.

An Agent asking to join gets a persistent card below the Header on its own name card (its mark, its name, the project and what access it asks for, Deny and Allow) that appears without a hover or click and without taking the keyboard; nothing dismisses it — no close action, outside press or Escape — and pressing a Header mark brings its Deny into keyboard reach without opening a dialog. An answer goes once and holds both choices until the list moves on to the next request; one that does not go through says so, stays answerable and lets nobody in. The server dropping a request (expired or answered elsewhere) ends it without a write, a failed refresh keeps it, a late answer changes nothing in another project, and losing the account forgets it.

The Header shows who is in the hosted Project: an Agent asking to join first, then whoever is at work, each its own mark (at most three), and everyone else as one stack of up to three faces with a count of the rest. A live mark is named by the Agent and what it is doing ("Claude Code · Wants to join", "Busy agent · Working now"); the stack is named by all of them as a sentence ("A, B, C, D, and E"). An Agent is drawn as the brand it chose when it connected ("other" being no brand, an unknown picture no choice), else the brand its name names, else its own creature from its name — never a letter — and only a working mark's creature is awake and hops, never for someone who asked for less motion. While nobody is here the empty seat opens the Agents dialog on the invite; once Agents are, the seat gives way and any mark or the stack opens the one dialog, remembering which opened it. Removing the last Agent from the dialog leaves the empty seat and the dialog open. Nothing is listed before the Project is known; someone the server will not show the Agents to is offered nothing about them, and there is no sharing with people.

Resting on a Header face shows its card after a moment (350 ms), hung from that face: when it last worked (Working now, Last worked 2 hours ago, No recent work), then the Agent, how it got in (Approved by you, Joined with a link) and how long it may stay (Access ends <date>, or Here since <date> when access does not end). Where the stack's faces overlap the card is the front face's; it then follows the pointer from face to face at once and leaves with it. The faces show no tooltip over the card. No card covers an open Agents dialog or a request's own card.

The Agents dialog, titled for the Project, meets everyone in one wrapping grid of equal seats with no sideways scrolling: an Agent asking to join first (let in or turned away where it stands), then the one at work ("Working now"), then the rest with only how long ago they last worked, and the invite seat last. While nobody is here it opens on the invite instead. Removing asks once on the tile; Keep takes nothing out; a removal or answer that does not go through says so and keeps the Agent. An invite is spent once it lets an Agent in, so there are no links to look after, and opening the dialog writes nothing; it closes from its own button or Escape.

Inviting starts from the seat at the end of the Agents and shows nothing until it is pressed. Nothing is made before Copy: the prompt reads true up to the link, which shows masked. Every Copy makes an invite of its own (a sign-in admission for the running workspace with a fresh pai_ secret) and copies one line naming the Project; the prompt then shows the link with its secret masked past its start, and a drawing of pasting with the paste keys plays another Agent each pass. An Agent asking to join takes the invite's place where it asks. An invite that could not be made says so and Copy works again; a refusal says only the owner may, copying nothing and setting no wait.

reason: TS closes the Agents dialog (and its invite) when an Agent asks to join, so the request's persistent card below the Header takes its place. The native Agents dialog stays open and answers the request where the Agent asks — in the invite's let-in step or at the front of the grid — and the Header's card waits until the dialog closes; a deliberate native design (qubits 966f415d2).

TS can show a hosted workspace at a Scope, whose Header then never asks for Agents. A native Cloud Project window always opens a whole Project (live Cloud files require project-root access, and a Scope checkout is never a hosted target), so there is no scoped hosted view whose Header could look for Agents.

TS's invite unfolds under the grid's seat with only its first step (copy the prompt), adds a second (paste it into the agent's chat, beside eight agent logos) after Copy, folds away on any press outside, is headed "Invite your first agent" while nobody is here, and aims its arrow at the seat. The native invite is the v4 two-step invite (qubits 966f415d2): it replaces the grid in the dialog, shows both steps from the start (send the prompt, then let the Agent in), keeps the first open on pasting with its drawing until the Agent asks, and ends with the Agent it brought in or when the dialog closes; there is no arrow, logo row or first-invite heading. The copy itself (one invite per Copy, the masked link, failure and refusal) is the same and mapped in cloud-agents-invite.
